**Sources.** Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), National Income and Product Accounts, via FRED: [Exports of goods and services (`EXPGSA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/EXPGSA),
[Imports of goods and services (`IMPGSA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IMPGSA) and [Gross domestic product (`GDPA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA).
Prepared file: [`data/ch19/us_trade.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/us_trade.csv), checked against [`data/ch19/fig19-1.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/fig19-1.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.1 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- In the 1950s exports and imports were each only about 4 to 5 percent of GDP. Since then exports have more than
  doubled and imports more than tripled.
- The two lines move together until the early 1970s, and then they separate: imports have been above exports every
  year since 1976. The gap between them is the trade deficit of Fig. 2.
- Trade falls sharply in world recessions (2009, 2020) and in the strong-dollar years of the mid-1980s, when U.S.
  exports dropped to 7 percent of GDP.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: how much does the United States trade?

The textbook says that exports and imports rose "from under 5 percent of GDP in the 1950s to around 12 and 15
percent of GDP, respectively, in recent years" (Jones 2024).

```{python}
# Step 1: the 1950s, and 2022, the textbook's last year.
# `.idxmax()` gives the label (here the year) of the largest value
fifties = shares.loc[1950:1959]
print(
    f"1950s: highest export share {fifties.Exports.max():.2f}% "
    f"({fifties.Exports.idxmax()}), "
    f"highest import share {fifties.Imports.max():.2f}%"
)
print(
    f"2022, the textbook's last year: exports {shares.Exports[2022]:.2f}%, "
    f"imports {shares.Imports[2022]:.2f}%"
)

# Step 2: since when have imports been above exports? `~` means "not": `~above`
# is True in the years when imports were not above exports
above = shares.Imports > shares.Exports
print(
    "Imports have been above exports every year since "
    f"{above[~above].index.max() + 1}"
)

# Step 3: openness, exports + imports as a percent of GDP
openness = shares.Exports + shares.Imports
print(
    f"Exports + imports: {openness[1950]:.1f}% of GDP in 1950, "
    f"{openness.max():.1f}% at the peak ({openness.idxmax()}), "
    f"{openness[last]:.1f}% in {last}"
)
```

The textbook's "respectively" lists the two numbers the wrong way round: exports are about 12 percent of GDP
(11.65 percent in 2022) and imports about 15 percent (15.18 percent). And "under 5 percent" holds only after rounding: exports
reached 5.07 percent in 1957. Exports and imports together, a common measure of how **open** an economy is, went
from 8 percent of GDP in 1950 to a peak of 30.8 percent in 2011.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond the United States: how open is each economy?

The textbook shows only the United States. The World Bank's *World Development Indicators* (WDI) publish the same
two shares, exports and imports of goods and services as a percent of GDP (series `NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS` and
`NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS`), for almost every economy. The file `wdi_trade.csv` has one row per economy and year from 1960 to
2025 (most economies start later, and 2025 is still missing for many). Its column `trade_balance` is exports minus
imports (`NE.RSB.GNFS.ZS`), which we use in Fig. 2. The small file `countries.csv` gives each economy's World Bank
region and income group.

```{python}
# Step 1: load the World Bank data (percent of GDP) and the groups of each economy
world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")
regions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")   # region and income group

# Step 2: compare the U.S. rows with the BEA data of Fig. 1: the WDI copy the
# BEA's numbers, so the two should agree. Subtracting two Series lines them up by
# their labels (the years), and a year that one of them lacks gives NaN, which
# `.max()` skips
us_wdi = world[world.country == "U.S."].set_index("year")
gap = max(
    (us_wdi.exports - shares.Exports).abs().max(),
    (us_wdi.imports - shares.Imports).abs().max(),
)
# `.nunique()` counts the different values in a column
print(
    f"{world.country.nunique()} economies, {world.year.min()}-{world.year.max()}; "
    f"the U.S. rows start in {us_wdi.index.min()} and differ from the BEA data "
    f"by at most {gap:.2f} points"
)
world.head()
```

Each economy gets one fixed color, so that it keeps its color when you add or remove others. Plotly offers 44 dark
enough colors, fewer than the 214 economies, so `group_colors` hands them out such that the economies of one menu
group (the G7, a region, ...) never share a color, as far as 44 colors allow.

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, the palette of country colors
# too pale on a white background
LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]
# 24 + 26 colors of two Plotly palettes, 44 of them kept
PALETTE = []
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if color not in LIGHT and color != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(color)
# Dark24's medium blue goes last: it is close to the book's navy
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, a color for every economy
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses.

    As far as the palette allows: when no color is free, the country gets the least
    used one, searched from the end of the palette.

    Arguments
        names  : the countries to color
        groups : the lists of countries shown together (the menu views)
        fixed  : {country: color} for the textbook countries, or None
    Returns
        a dictionary {country: color}
    """
    # start from a copy of the fixed colors (or an empty dictionary)
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in sorted(names):
        if name in colors:
            continue                    # `continue` skips to the next country
        # Step 1: `score` gives every color a cost (lower is better): 1 for each
        # country that already uses it anywhere
        score = {}
        for color in PALETTE:
            score[color] = list(colors.values()).count(color)
        # Step 2: 10 for each country of a large group that uses it (Europe has
        # more countries than there are colors), and 100 for each one of a group
        # small enough to avoid any clash. `a if test else b` gives a when the
        # test is True and b otherwise; `colors.get(other)` is None for a country
        # without a color yet
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                weight = 100 if len(group) <= len(PALETTE) else 10
                for other in group:
                    if colors.get(other) in score:
                        score[colors[other]] += weight
        # Step 3: `min(PALETTE, key=score.get)` picks the color with the lowest
        # cost (the first one on ties)
        best = min(PALETTE, key=score.get)
        # no free color: the least used one, searching from the end of the list
        # (`PALETTE[::-1]` is the list in reverse order), so that the leftovers
        # take the last, rarely used colors
        if score[best] >= 10:
            best = min(PALETTE[::-1], key=score.get)
        colors[name] = best
    return colors


# The color of every economy; the U.S. keeps the book's blue
COLORS = group_colors(
    regions.country,
    country_groups(regions, ["U.S."]).values(),
    {"U.S.": BLUE},
)
```

The dictionary `COLORS` maps each economy to its color, and `color_discrete_map=COLORS` makes Plotly use it, in Colab
and on the website. `fit_range` keeps the textbook's axis range when the data fit in it; otherwise it returns `None`,
which lets Plotly choose a range that shows every value.

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Figs. 1 to 6, the textbook's axis range when the data fit
def fit_range(values, book_range):
    """The textbook's axis range if every value fits in it, otherwise None.

    With None, Plotly chooses a range that shows every value.

    Arguments
        values     : the values drawn on the axis
        book_range : [lowest, highest], the textbook's range
    Returns
        book_range, or None
    """
    # every value between the lowest and the highest end of the textbook's range
    if values.min() >= book_range[0] and values.max() <= book_range[1]:
        return book_range
    # some value would fall off the chart: let Plotly choose
    return None
```

The figure draws Fig. 19.1 for any list of economies. First the data: `trade_shares_data` keeps the rows of the
chosen economies and computes exports plus imports, the **openness** of each economy, in its latest year. The
title of the figure reports it.

```{python}
# The flows that the buttons of the figure can show
FLOWS = {
    "Exports and imports": ["Exports", "Imports"],
    "Exports": ["Exports"],
    "Imports": ["Imports"],
}


def trade_shares_data(countries, flow):
    """The data of Fig. 1 for any economies, and the openness of each.

    Openness: exports + imports, percent of GDP, in each economy's latest year.

    Arguments
        countries : the economies to show
        flow      : a key of FLOWS, the flows to show
    Returns
        rows     : the chosen economies' rows of `world`
        long     : the flows to draw, one row per economy, year and flow
        openness : each economy's exports + imports in its latest year
    """
    # Step 1: `.isin(countries)` is True for the rows whose economy is in the
    # list; `.rename(columns={...})` gives the columns readable names
    rows = world[world.country.isin(countries)].rename(
        columns={"exports": "Exports", "imports": "Imports"}
    )
    # Step 2: `.melt(...)` stacks the export and import columns into one column
    # `share`, with a new column `flow` that says which is which
    long = rows.melt(
        id_vars=["country", "year"],
        value_vars=FLOWS[flow],
        var_name="flow",
        value_name="share",
    )
    # Step 3: `.groupby("country").last()` keeps each economy's last row with
    # both flows; openness is exports + imports in that year
    last = rows.dropna(subset=["Exports", "Imports"]).groupby("country").last()
    openness = last.Exports + last.Imports
    return rows, long, openness
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1 for any economies
def trade_shares_world(countries=("U.S.",), flow="Exports and imports"):
    """Exports and imports, percent of GDP (World Bank WDI), for any economies.

    Draws Fig. 1 (inspired by Fig. 19.1 in Jones) for any list of economies.

    Arguments
        countries : the economies to show
        flow      : "Exports and imports", "Exports" or "Imports"
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (trade_shares_data)
    rows, long, openness = trade_shares_data(countries, flow)
    if len(rows) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Choose at least one economy"))

    # Step 2: the title names two economies and counts the rest.
    # `", ".join(names)` glues a list of texts together
    names = []
    for name in openness.index[:2]:
        names.append(f"{name} {openness[name]:.0f}%")
    more = f" + {len(openness) - 2} more" if len(openness) > 2 else ""

    # Step 3: one line per economy and flow: `line_dash="flow"` draws exports
    # solid and imports dashed, and `color_discrete_map=COLORS` gives each
    # economy its own color, in Colab and on the website
    fig = px.line(
        long,
        x="year",
        y="share",
        color="country",
        line_dash="flow",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        labels={"year": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "flow": "Flow"},
        title="Latest exports + imports, % of GDP: " + ", ".join(names) + more,
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)

    # Step 4: the axes: the textbook's range when the data fit in it
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1955, 2027])         # 1960 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(long.share.dropna(), [2, 18.5]))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget

# into a widget, and draws the figure again every time you change one; the `;` at

);
```

The United States is one of the **least open** economies in the world: in 2024 only four of 172 economies traded
less relative to their GDP. Large economies trade less, because much of their trade happens inside their own
borders. Small trading hubs such as Singapore (313 percent) and Luxembourg (351 percent) import goods and
re-export them, so their exports and imports can each exceed GDP.

### Fig. 2: The U.S. trade balance as a share of GDP

**Goal.** Measure the U.S. trade deficit and test the rule that trade must balance in the long run.

The trade balance is exports minus imports. We compute it with `net_exports`, turn it into a share of GDP, and check
it against the figure's data file, which was computed from the BEA's own net-exports series.

```{python}
# The trade balance NX = EX - IM, as a percent of GDP
us["trade_balance"] = share_of_gdp(net_exports(us.exports, us.imports), us.gdp)
# the check against the figure's data file: the largest gap, in points
check = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig19-2.csv").set_index("year")
print(
    "Largest difference from fig19-2.csv: "
    f"{(us.trade_balance - check.trade_balance_pct_gdp).abs().max():.4f} points"
)
us.trade_balance.loc[[1950, 1975, 1976, 1987, 2006, 2025]].round(2)
```

The Oddtopia example says that the trade balance must average zero over a long period. `balance_window` computes
the average trade balance over a window of years, using our `period_average`, and counts the deficit years in it.
The figure shades that window and reports both numbers.

```{python}
def balance_window(start, end):
    """The average U.S. trade balance over a window of years, and its deficit years.

    Fig. 2:  the average of 100 NX / Y from start to end (period_average)

    Arguments
        start, end : the first and the last year of the window
    Returns
        start, end : the same two years, in order (start <= end)
        avg        : the average trade balance, percent of GDP
        deficits   : the number of years with a deficit, NX < 0
    """
    # `min(a, b)` and `max(a, b)` give the smaller and the larger of two numbers,
    # so the window stays valid even if the two sliders cross
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)
    avg = period_average(us.trade_balance, start, end)
    # `(series < 0).sum()` counts the deficit years, because each True counts as 1
    deficits = (us.trade_balance.loc[start:end] < 0).sum()
    return start, end, avg, deficits
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2, the U.S. trade balance
def trade_balance_chart(start=1976, end=2025):
    """The U.S. trade balance (percent of GDP), with its average from start to end.

    Draws Fig. 2 (inspired by Fig. 19.2 in Jones).

    Arguments
        start, end : the first and the last year of the shaded window
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (balance_window)
    start, end, avg, deficits = balance_window(start, end)

    # Step 2: the trade balance, year by year; the title reports the window
    fig = px.line(
        us.reset_index(),
        x="year",
        y="trade_balance",
        color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
        labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"},
        title=(
            f"{start}–{end}: average trade balance {avg:+.2f}% of GDP, "
            f"deficits in {deficits} of {end - start + 1} years"
        ),
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)

    # Step 3: the zero line; `add_vrect` shades the window between two x values,
    # and `add_shape(type="line", ...)` draws the dotted average as one segment
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.add_shape(
        type="line",
        x0=start,
        x1=end,
        y0=avg,
        y1=avg,
        line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3, dash="dot"),
    )

    # Step 4: what the two sides of zero mean
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=1990,
        y=1.6,
        text="Above zero: exports > imports",
        showarrow=False,
        font=dict(size=13),
    )
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=1965,
        y=-4.5,
        text="Below zero: imports > exports",
        showarrow=False,
        font=dict(size=13),
    )

    # Step 5: the textbook's axes, with no tick label in the corner
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1948, 2027])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-6.5, 2.5], tickvals=[-5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2])
    return fig
```

Prepared file: [`data/ch19/us_trade.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/us_trade.csv), checked against [`data/ch19/fig19-2.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/fig19-2.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.2 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- From 1950 to 1975 the United States usually had a small surplus (the dotted average line is above zero for that
  window). After 1975 the pattern reversed: there has not been a single surplus year since.
- The deficit grew in two waves, to about 3 percent of GDP in 1987 and to 5.7 percent in 2006, and has stayed near
  3 percent since 2009. The dotted line is the average over the shaded years.
- Over the whole period 1950–2025 the average is still negative, about −1.5 percent of GDP. Trade has not
  balanced yet: according to the Oddtopia example, the rest of the world expects future U.S. surpluses.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: the deficit in the text

```{python}
# Step 1: 1950 to 1975: the surplus years and the deficit years
tb = us.trade_balance
early = tb.loc[1950:1975]
print(
    f"1950-1975: surplus in {(early > 0).sum()} of {len(early)} years; "
    f"deficits in {list(early[early < 0].index)}"
)

# Step 2: the surplus years since 1976 (none), and the largest deficit;
# `.idxmin()` gives the year of the smallest value
print(f"Surplus years after 1975: {list(tb.loc[1976:][tb.loc[1976:] > 0].index)}")
print(f"Largest deficit: {tb.min():.2f}% of GDP in {tb.idxmin()}")

# Step 3: the range since 2000, and the recent average
print(
    f"2000-2022: from {tb.loc[2000:2022].min():.2f}% "
    f"to {tb.loc[2000:2022].max():.2f}% of GDP"
)
print(f"Average 2023-2025: {period_average(tb, 2023, 2025):.2f}% of GDP")

# Step 4: equation (1): C + I + G = Y - NX, here 100 - NX in percent of GDP
print(f"2006: domestic uses C + I + G were {100 - tb[2006]:.1f}% of GDP (equation 1)")
```

The text's numbers hold: a surplus in 23 of the 26 years from 1950 to 1975, no surplus since, a deficit of 5.7
percent in 2006 (the text says 5.6; the data have been revised since) and about 3 percent in recent years. In 2006,
Americans consumed, invested and bought through their governments 105.7 percent of what they produced.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond the United States: who runs deficits, who runs surpluses?

Does trade balance in the long run in other countries? The same figure, for any economy, uses the WDI trade balance
of `wdi_trade.csv`. The dotted lines are each economy's average over the chosen years.

Both functions of this figure are drawing code: `add_average` draws an economy's average as a dotted segment,
and `trade_balance_world` draws the trade balance of each chosen economy with its average. The only economics
in them is the average itself, which comes from our `period_average`.

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2, the dotted average line of each economy
def add_average(fig, series, name, start, end):
    """Draw the average of a yearly series from start to end as a dotted segment.

    The dotted lines of Fig. 2 for any economies; period_average gives the average.

    Arguments
        fig        : the Plotly figure to draw on
        series     : a yearly series, with the years as labels
        name       : the economy, for its color and its legend group
        start, end : the first and the last year of the window
    Returns
        the average (NaN when the window has no data)
    """
    avg = period_average(series, start, end)
    # NaN (no data in the window) is not equal to itself
    if avg == avg:
        # `go.Scatter(..., mode="lines")` with two points draws one straight
        # segment. `legendgroup=name` ties it to the economy's line, so that a
        # click on the legend hides both, and `showlegend=False` keeps it out of
        # the legend
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=[start, end],
                y=[avg, avg],
                mode="lines",
                name=name + ", average",
                legendgroup=name,
                showlegend=False,
                line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=3, dash="dot"),
            )
        )
    return avg
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2 for any economies
def trade_balance_world(countries=("U.S.",), start=1976, end=2024):
    """The trade balance (percent of GDP, WDI) and its average from start to end.

    Draws Fig. 2 (inspired by Fig. 19.2 in Jones) for any economies.

    Arguments
        countries  : the economies to show
        start, end : the first and the last year of the averages
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the window, in order even if the sliders cross, and the chosen rows
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)
    rows = world[world.country.isin(countries)]

    # Step 2: one line per economy, in its own color
    fig = px.line(
        rows,
        x="year",
        y="trade_balance",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"},
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)

    # Step 3: each economy's dotted average (add_average), and its text for the
    # title
    names = []
    for name in sorted(set(rows.country)):
        series = rows[rows.country == name].set_index("year").trade_balance
        avg = add_average(fig, series, name, start, end)
        if avg == avg:
            # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
            names.append(f"{name} {round(avg, 1) + 0.0:+.1f}%")
        else:
            names.append(f"{name}: no data")

    # Step 4: the title names two economies and counts the rest
    more = f" + {len(names) - 2} more" if len(names) > 2 else ""
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"Average trade balance {start}–{end}: " + ", ".join(names[:2]) + more,
        legend_title_text="",
    )

    # Step 5: the zero line, the shaded window and the axes
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1955, 2027])         # 1960 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(rows.trade_balance.dropna(), [-6.5, 2.5]))
    return fig
```

### Fig. 3: The trade balance around the world

**Goal.** Find the countries whose trade surpluses mirror the U.S. trade deficit.

For the world as a whole, trade must balance: every import is someone else's export. So the U.S. deficit must show
up as surpluses elsewhere. The Penn World Table (PWT) compares countries at the same prices (purchasing power
parity, PPP). The file `pwt_trade.csv` holds, for nine countries, the GDP shares of consumption (`csh_c`),
investment (`csh_i`) and government purchases (`csh_g`), and GDP at PPP (`cgdpo`, in millions of US dollars), in two
versions of the table: PWT 10.01, the one the textbook used, which ends in 2019, and PWT 11.0, which runs to 2023.

```{python}
# Load the nine textbook countries. A new column made from other columns is
# computed for every row at once: our function `trade_balance_share` applies
# 100 (1 - c - i - g), equation (2), to all 576 rows
pwt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_trade.csv")
pwt["trade_balance"] = trade_balance_share(pwt.csh_c, pwt.csh_i, pwt.csh_g)
pwt.head()
```

The file `pwt_trade_world.csv` has the same columns for **every** country in PWT 11.0 (185 economies, 1990 to 2023),
plus real GDP (`rgdpna`, millions of 2021 US dollars) and population (`pop`, millions), which we use after Fig. 4.
Its rows for the nine textbook countries are identical to those of `pwt_trade.csv`. PWT 10.01 is kept only for the
nine countries, to check the textbook.

```{python}
# Every economy of PWT 11.0, with the same trade balance
pwt_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_trade_world.csv")
pwt_world["trade_balance"] = trade_balance_share(
    pwt_world.csh_c, pwt_world.csh_i, pwt_world.csh_g
)
print(
    f"{pwt_world.country.nunique()} economies, "
    f"{pwt_world.year.min()}-{pwt_world.year.max()}"
)
```

The second bar of the textbook's figure shows each country's trade balance as a share of **U.S.** GDP, so the bars
of different countries can be added up and compared with the U.S. deficit: we multiply the share of own GDP by the
country's GDP and divide by U.S. GDP.

You can add any country to the figure. `book_order` keeps the textbook's countries first and says which chosen
countries have no data (PWT 10.01 has only the nine textbook countries).

```{python}
# The textbook's five countries of Fig. 3, in its order
FIG3 = ["U.S.", "Japan", "China", "France", "Germany"]


def book_order(countries, book, available):
    """The chosen countries with data, the textbook's first, and those without data.

    The textbook's countries come in its order, then the others from A to Z.

    Arguments
        countries : the chosen countries
        book      : the textbook's countries, in its order
        available : the countries that have data
    Returns
        order   : the chosen countries with data
        missing : the chosen countries without data
    """
    order, missing = [], []
    for name in list(book) + sorted(countries):
        # each chosen country once
        if name in countries and name not in order and name not in missing:
            if name in available:
                order.append(name)
            else:
                missing.append(name)
    # a function can `return` two results at once; the caller unpacks them into
    # two names: `order, missing = book_order(...)`
    return order, missing
```

The two bars of each country are the economics of Fig. 3: its trade balance as a share of its own GDP, and
the same balance as a share of U.S. GDP, from `share_of_us_gdp`. `world_balance_data` computes them for one
year and one version of the table.

```{python}
def world_balance_data(year, vintage, countries):
    """The two bars of Fig. 3 for each chosen country, in one year.

    Fig. 3:  100 NX / Y, and the same as a share of U.S. GDP, 100 NX / Y_US

    Arguments
        year      : the year
        vintage   : "PWT 11.0" or "PWT 10.01", the version of the table
        countries : the chosen countries
    Returns
        year    : the year shown (PWT 10.01 ends in 2019)
        bars    : one row per country: the trade balance as a percent of its own
                  GDP and as a percent of U.S. GDP
        missing : the chosen countries without data
    """
    # Step 1: the table of that version, and the year (PWT 10.01 ends in 2019)
    source = pwt_world if vintage == "PWT 11.0" else pwt
    year = min(year, source[source.vintage == vintage].year.max())
    rows = source[(source.year == year) & (source.vintage == vintage)]
    rows = rows.set_index("country")
    # Step 2: the chosen countries with data, the textbook's first
    order, missing = book_order(countries, FIG3, rows.index)
    one = rows.loc[order]
    # Step 3: the two bars: a share of own GDP, and a share of U.S. GDP
    bars = pd.DataFrame({
        "Share of own GDP": one.trade_balance,
        "Share of U.S. GDP": share_of_us_gdp(
            one.trade_balance, one.cgdpo, rows.loc["U.S.", "cgdpo"]
        ),
    })
    return year, bars, missing
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, the title
def world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing):
    """The title of Fig. 3: the U.S. deficit and the largest surplus.

    The surplus in percent of U.S. GDP; a note instead when a chosen country has no
    data.

    Arguments
        year    : the year shown
        vintage : the version of the Penn World Table
        bars    : the two bars of each country (world_balance_data)
        missing : the chosen countries without data
    Returns
        the title, a text
    """
    # Step 1: a note when some chosen country has no data, or none is chosen
    if missing:
        return f"{year}: no {vintage} data for " + ", ".join(missing[:3])
    if len(bars) == 0:
        return "Choose at least one country"
    # Step 2: the year and the U.S. deficit, in percent of U.S. GDP
    text = f"{year} ({vintage}): "
    if "U.S." in bars.index:
        text += f"U.S. deficit {-bars.loc['U.S.', 'Share of own GDP']:.1f}% of GDP; "
    # the country with the largest balance in percent of U.S. GDP; + 0.0 turns
    # -0.0 into 0.0
    top = bars["Share of U.S. GDP"].idxmax()
    value = round(bars.loc[top, "Share of U.S. GDP"], 2) + 0.0
    # Step 3: a surplus if the largest balance is positive, else a deficit
    if value > 0:
        return text + f"largest surplus {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"
    return text + f"smallest deficit {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, the trade balance around the world
def world_balance_chart(year=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0", countries=FIG3):
    """The trade balance as a share of own GDP and of U.S. GDP, in one year.

    Draws Fig. 3 (inspired by Fig. 19.3 in Jones).

    Arguments
        year      : the year
        vintage   : "PWT 11.0" or "PWT 10.01", the version of the table
        countries : the countries to show
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the two bars of each country (world_balance_data)
    year, bars, missing = world_balance_data(year, vintage, countries)

    # Step 2: `.melt(id_vars="country")` turns the two measure columns into rows,
    # one row per country and measure: the long shape that `px.bar` needs
    long = bars.reset_index().melt(
        id_vars="country",
        var_name="Measure",
        value_name="Percent",
    )

    # Step 3: with `color="Measure"` and `barmode="group"`, the two bars of each
    # country stand side by side
    fig = px.bar(
        long,
        x="country",
        y="Percent",
        color="Measure",
        barmode="group",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map={"Share of own GDP": BLUE, "Share of U.S. GDP": GREEN},
        labels={"country": "", "Percent": "Percent"},
        title=world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing),
    )
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)

    # Step 4: the textbook's range, unless a bar does not fit
    book = fit_range(long.Percent, [-9, 12.5])
    if book:
        fig.update_yaxes(
            range=book,
            tickvals=[-8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12],
        )
    fig.update_layout(
        legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", title="")
    )
    return fig
```

(GDP at current PPPs). Prepared files: [`data/ch19/pwt_trade.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/pwt_trade.csv) and [`data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.3 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- The United States has a deficit in every year, and France in every year since 2006. China and Germany run
  surpluses in every year, and Japan in 19 of the 24 years, as in the textbook.
- Measured in U.S. GDP (green bars), China's surplus has been the largest since 2005; before that Japan's or
  Germany's was. Germany's surplus is large relative to its own economy, but Germany is much smaller than the United
  States, so its green bar is short.
- In PWT 11.0 China's economy at PPP has been larger than the U.S. economy since 2017, so China's green bar is now
  taller than its blue bar. Choose PWT 10.01 and 2017 to see the textbook's figure.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: which year did the textbook plot?

The textbook's figure is titled 2019, and the text says that "the U.S. trade deficit that year was about 4 percent of
GDP". The values below are read off the textbook's bars.

```{python}
# Step 1: the textbook's bars, read off its figure
book = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Share of own GDP": [-4.0, 1.8, 3.0, -2.9, 7.0],
        "Share of U.S. GDP": [-4.0, 0.45, 3.05, -0.45, 1.5],
    },
    index=FIG3,
)

# Step 2: next to them, the trade balance in PWT 10.01 (2017 and 2019) and in
# PWT 11.0 (2019)
compare = pd.DataFrame({"Textbook": book["Share of own GDP"]})
for year in [2017, 2019]:
    one = pwt[(pwt.year == year) & (pwt.vintage == "PWT 10.01")].set_index("country")
    compare[f"PWT 10.01, {year}"] = one.trade_balance
compare["PWT 11.0, 2019"] = (
    pwt[(pwt.year == 2019) & (pwt.vintage == "PWT 11.0")]
    .set_index("country")
    .trade_balance
)
compare.round(2)
```

The 2017 values of PWT 10.01 reproduce the textbook's bars within 0.05 points; the 2019 values do not (Germany 5.3,
not 7.0; China 2.1, not 3.0). So the textbook's bars are **2017** data under a 2019 title, probably left over from
an earlier edition. And a newer version of the same table changes the numbers again: in PWT 11.0, Japan's 2019
surplus is almost zero. **Always check which year, and which version of a dataset, a figure really shows.**

```{python}
# The U.S. deficit and the other four balances, in percent of U.S. GDP
for vintage, year in [("PWT 10.01", 2017), ("PWT 11.0", 2023)]:
    one = pwt[(pwt.year == year) & (pwt.vintage == vintage)].set_index("country")
    one = one.loc[FIG3]
    in_us_gdp = share_of_us_gdp(one.trade_balance, one.cgdpo, one.loc["U.S.", "cgdpo"])
    print(
        f"{year} ({vintage}): U.S. deficit {-in_us_gdp['U.S.']:.2f}% of U.S. GDP; "
        f"surpluses of the other four together {in_us_gdp.drop('U.S.').sum():.2f}%"
    )
```

The four other countries' balances together are about as large as the whole U.S. deficit. China alone covers most
of it.

## Trade and growth around the world

Should fast-growing countries borrow from abroad to invest? Here we check whether the fastest growers really run trade deficits.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 4: The trade balance in rapidly growing countries

**Goal.** Test whether fast-growing countries borrow from abroad, as consumption smoothing predicts.

A country that expects to be much richer tomorrow should borrow today, like a student who expects a high income
later: it should run trade **deficits**. The textbook checks this for five fast-growing economies. Each bar is the
simple average of the yearly trade balance over a window of years. We first make a table with one row per year and
one column per country, so that `period_average` gives one average per country.

```{python}
# The textbook's five fast-growing economies, and their rows of both PWT versions
FIG4 = ["China", "India", "Singapore", "Ireland", "S. Korea"]
fast = pwt[pwt.country.isin(FIG4)]


def fast_growers_data(start, end, vintage, countries):
    """The bars of Fig. 4: each economy's average trade balance over a window.

    Fig. 4:  the average of 100 NX / Y from start to end (period_average)

    Arguments
        start, end : the first and the last year of the window
        vintage    : "PWT 11.0" or "PWT 10.01", the version of the table
        countries  : the chosen economies
    Returns
        end     : the last year used (PWT 10.01 ends in 2019)
        avg     : each economy's average trade balance, percent of own GDP
        missing : the chosen economies without data
    """
    # Step 1: one row per year and one column per country, with `.pivot(...)`
    source = pwt_world if vintage == "PWT 11.0" else pwt
    wide = source[source.vintage == vintage].pivot(
        index="year",
        columns="country",
        values="trade_balance",
    )
    end = min(end, wide.index.max())                 # PWT 10.01 ends in 2019
    # Step 2: the chosen economies, the textbook's first: `wide[order]` keeps
    # their columns in that order, and period_average gives one average each
    order, missing = book_order(countries, FIG4, wide.columns)
    avg = period_average(wide[order], start, end)
    return end, avg, missing
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, the trade balance in rapidly growing countries
def fast_growers_chart(start=2000, end=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0", countries=FIG4):
    """The average trade balance (percent of own GDP) of fast-growing economies.

    Draws Fig. 4 (inspired by Fig. 19.4 in Jones), for the textbook's five or any
    chosen economies.

    Arguments
        start, end : the first and the last year of the averages
        vintage    : "PWT 11.0" or "PWT 10.01", the version of the table
        countries  : the economies to show
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the averages (fast_growers_data), and the title
    end, avg, missing = fast_growers_data(start, end, vintage, countries)
    bars = avg.rename("average").reset_index()
    title = (
        f"{start}–{end} ({vintage}): {(avg > 0).sum()} of {len(avg)} economies "
        "ran trade surpluses on average"
    )
    if missing:
        title = f"{start}–{end}: no {vintage} data for " + ", ".join(missing[:3])

    # Step 2: one bar per economy; `text_auto=".1f"` writes each bar's value, with
    # one decimal, on the bar
    fig = px.bar(
        bars,
        x="country",
        y="average",
        text_auto=".1f",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN],
        labels={"country": "", "average": "Percent of own GDP"},
        title=title,
    )
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)

    # Step 3: the textbook's range, unless a bar does not fit
    book = fit_range(avg.dropna(), [-5, 30])
    if book:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=book, tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30])
    return fig
```

Prepared files: [`data/ch19/pwt_trade.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/pwt_trade.csv) and [`data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.4 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- With one exception, India, these fast-growing economies run trade **surpluses**, not deficits. They lend to the
  rest of the world instead of borrowing from it.
- This is the opposite of what consumption smoothing (the permanent-income idea of Chapter 16) predicts. The textbook
  suggests that the causality may run the other way: countries that push their firms to export may grow faster.
- Singapore's and Ireland's averages are very sensitive to the window. Move the first year back to 1990: Singapore's
  average falls from 19.3 to 10.6 percent. The next subsection shows why.

<!-- cell -->

#### Look at your data: an average can hide big swings

We draw the yearly balances behind the averages, in PWT 11.0, and find the lowest and the highest of them.

```{python}
# The yearly trade balances of the five in PWT 11.0, and the rows of the lowest
# and the highest (`.idxmin()` and `.idxmax()` give their row labels)
annual = fast[fast.vintage == "PWT 11.0"]
low = annual.loc[annual.trade_balance.idxmin()]
high = annual.loc[annual.trade_balance.idxmax()]
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing

# one line per country; the title reports the lowest and the highest balance
fig = px.line(
    annual,
    x="year",
    y="trade_balance",
    color="country",
    hover_name="country",
    color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GRAY, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8"],
    labels={
        "year": "Year",
        "trade_balance": "Percent of own GDP",
        "country": "Country",
    },
    title=(
        f"Yearly trade balances swing: {low.country} {low.trade_balance:.1f}% "
        f"in {low.year}, {high.country} {high.trade_balance:.1f}% in {high.year}"
    ),
)
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
```

**Sources.** Data: Groningen Growth and Development Centre, [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) ([doi:10.34894/FABVLR](https://doi.org/10.34894/FABVLR)) (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015, *American Economic Review*); variables `csh_c`, `csh_i` and `csh_g`.
Prepared file: [`data/ch19/pwt_trade.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/pwt_trade.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.4 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

Two series behave strangely. Singapore's balance jumps from −33 percent of GDP in 1993 to +15 percent in 1998.
Singapore is a trading hub: in the Penn World Table its exports and its imports were each about two to three times its
GDP in the mid-1990s, so its trade balance is a small difference between two huge numbers, and a small error in
either one moves it a lot. Ireland's balance swings from 32 percent of GDP in 2018 to 7 percent in 2019 and 50 percent in 2022: large
multinational firms book much of their production and profits in Ireland, which moves its GDP and trade statistics
far more than Irish living standards. Neither country's data are "wrong", but a single average hides all this, and
it changes a lot with the choice of years. That is why the figure lets you choose the window.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: which window did the textbook average?

The textbook's title says 2000–2019 and its text says "from 1990 to 2019". The values below are read off its bars.

```{python}
# Step 1: the textbook's bars, read off its figure
book4 = pd.Series([2.9, -0.4, 16.1, 22.8, 3.5], index=FIG4)
# Step 2: the five in PWT 10.01: one row per year, one column per country
wide10 = fast[fast.vintage == "PWT 10.01"].pivot(
    index="year",
    columns="country",
    values="trade_balance",
)
# Step 3: the averages over three windows, next to the textbook's bars
windows = pd.DataFrame({"Textbook": book4})
for start, end in [(2000, 2017), (2000, 2019), (1990, 2019)]:
    windows[f"PWT 10.01, {start}–{end}"] = period_average(wide10, start, end)
windows.round(2)
```

Only the window 2000–2017 reproduces the bars, within 0.05 points: like Fig. 3, the figure uses the data up to
2017. The text's window, 1990–2019, would give Singapore 7.6 instead of 16.1. The finding itself does not depend on
the window: India is the only deficit country in every column.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond the textbook's five: do fast-growing economies borrow?

The textbook picked five fast-growing economies. A fairer test uses **every** economy: does faster growth go with
smaller trade balances (borrowing), as consumption smoothing predicts? We measure growth of real GDP per person,
`rgdpna / pop`, from 2000 to 2023, and the average trade balance over the same years.

```{python}
def growth_rate(y, start, end):
    """The average annual growth rate between two years, in percent.

    The growth formula of Chapter 3:  100 ln(y_end / y_start) / (end - start)

    Arguments
        y          : a table whose rows are years (here one column per economy)
        start, end : the first and the last year
    Returns
        the average annual growth rate of each column, in percent
    """
    # `np.log` is the natural logarithm; the formula works on every column of the
    # wide table at once
    return 100 * np.log(y.loc[end] / y.loc[start]) / (end - start)


# Step 1: real GDP per person, then one row per year and one column per economy
pwt_world["gdp_per_person"] = pwt_world.rgdpna / pwt_world["pop"]
income = pwt_world.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdp_per_person")
balance = pwt_world.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance")

# Step 2: growth and the average trade balance, 2000-2023, in one table;
# `.dropna()` drops the economies that miss either one
growers = pd.DataFrame({
    "growth": growth_rate(income, 2000, 2023),
    "trade_balance": period_average(balance, 2000, 2023),
}).dropna().reset_index()
growers.sort_values("trade_balance").head(7).round(1)
```

**Look at your data.** A few small island economies have average "balances" of −40 to −2,200 percent of GDP
(Bermuda). These are not real trade deficits: PWT's consumption and investment shares are badly measured for such tiny,
finance-heavy economies. We set aside the economies beyond ±40 percent and say so.

```{python}
# Step 1: set aside the economies whose average balance is beyond 40 percent of
# GDP, up or down, and say which
odd = growers[growers.trade_balance.abs() > 40]
print(f"Set aside: {', '.join(odd.country)}")
growers = growers[growers.trade_balance.abs() <= 40].copy()

# Step 2: a group for the legend (`.map({...})` replaces True and False by the
# group names), and a label for the textbook's five only:
# `np.where(test, a, b)` takes a where the test is True and b elsewhere
growers["group"] = growers.country.isin(FIG4).map(
    {True: "Textbook's five", False: "Other economies"}
)
growers["label"] = np.where(growers.country.isin(FIG4), growers.country, "")

# Step 3: the least-squares line of the trade balance against growth: its slope
# is the change in the trade balance per point of faster growth
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(growers.growth, growers.trade_balance, 1)
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, growth and the trade balance in every economy
# Step 1: one point per economy. `trendline="ols"` with
# `trendline_scope="overall"` fits one straight line through all the points,
# whatever their color
fig = px.scatter(
    growers,
    x="growth",
    y="trade_balance",
    color="group",
    text="label",
    hover_name="country",
    trendline="ols",
    trendline_scope="overall",
    color_discrete_map={"Textbook's five": GREEN, "Other economies": GRAY},
    labels={
        "growth": "Growth of GDP per person, 2000–2023 (% a year)",
        "trade_balance": "Average trade balance (% of GDP)",
        "group": "",
    },
    title=(
        f"{len(growers)} economies: 1 point faster growth, "
        f"{slope:+.1f} points of trade balance"
    ),
)
# Step 2: the labels above the points, and the fitted line in blue
fig.update_traces(textposition="top center", marker_size=9)
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), selector=dict(mode="lines"))
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
fig.show()
# Step 3: below the chart, the correlation of growth and the trade balance, a
# number between -1 and +1 (`a.corr(b)` is the correlation of two columns)
print(f"Correlation: {growers.growth.corr(growers.trade_balance):.2f}")
```

**Sources.** Data: Groningen Growth and Development Centre, [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) ([doi:10.34894/FABVLR](https://doi.org/10.34894/FABVLR)) (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015, *American Economic Review*); variables `csh_c`, `csh_i`, `csh_g`, `rgdpna` (real GDP) and `pop`
(population). Prepared file: [`data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.4 and the discussion in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- Across all economies the fitted line slopes **down**: economies that grew faster ran smaller trade balances on
  average, as consumption smoothing predicts. But the link is weak (a correlation of about −0.2), and many fast
  growers sit on both sides of zero.
- The textbook's five are not typical. Of the 28 economies that grew faster than 4 percent a year, only 5 ran
  surpluses on average; many of the others (Ethiopia, Cambodia, Armenia) borrowed from abroad or received aid.
- So the textbook's puzzle is mostly a puzzle about East Asian exporters and Ireland. A data science lesson: a
  conclusion drawn from five hand-picked countries can change when you look at all of them.

## The twin deficits

The identity $NX = S - I$ links the trade balance to saving. This section compares the U.S. budget deficit, investment and the trade deficit over time.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 5: U.S. investment, budget deficit, and trade deficit

**Goal.** See the **twin deficits**: large budget deficits that come with large trade deficits.

Equation (4) says $NX = S - I$: a country that saves less than it invests must borrow the difference abroad. When
the government runs a larger budget deficit, government saving $T - G$ falls, and so does domestic saving $S$. Either
investment falls too, or foreigners fill the gap and the trade deficit grows. The file has the three series of the
textbook's figure, as percent of GDP.

```{python}
# Load the three series of Fig. 5, percent of GDP
twin = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig19-5.csv").set_index("year")
twin.head()
```

The trade **deficit** is minus the trade balance, so $NX = -$(trade deficit). With our function `domestic_saving` we
add a fourth line, domestic saving $S = I + NX$. The gap between saving and investment is then exactly the trade
deficit.

```{python}
# Step 1: readable column names, which then appear in the legend;
# `.rename(columns={...})` renames the columns
named = twin.rename(
    columns={
        "investment_pct_gdp": "Investment",
        "budget_deficit_pct_gdp": "Budget deficit",
        "trade_deficit_pct_gdp": "Trade deficit",
    }
)
# Step 2: domestic saving S = I + NX, equation (4), with NX = -(trade deficit)
named["Domestic saving, S = I + NX"] = domestic_saving(
    named.Investment, -named["Trade deficit"]
)
# Step 3: check that S - I equals minus the trade deficit in every year
gap = net_capital_outflow(named["Domestic saving, S = I + NX"], named.Investment)
print(
    "S - I equals minus the trade deficit in every year: "
    f"{((gap + named['Trade deficit']).abs() < 1e-9).all()}"
)
named.loc[[1979, 1986, 2006, 2025]].round(2)
```

The menu chooses an episode with a rising budget deficit. `episode_change` computes how much each line changed
between the first and the last year of the episode, and the title of the figure reports it.

```{python}
# The episodes of the menu, each with its first and last year
EPISODES = {
    "1980s: 1979 to 1986": (1979, 1986),
    "2000s: 2000 to 2006": (2000, 2006),
    "Great Recession: 2007 to 2010": (2007, 2010),
    "Covid-19: 2019 to 2021": (2019, 2021),
}
# the four lines of the figure
LINES = ["Investment", "Budget deficit", "Trade deficit", "Domestic saving, S = I + NX"]


def episode_change(episode):
    """The change of each line of Fig. 5 over one episode, in points of GDP.

    Fig. 5:  the value in the last year minus the value in the first year

    Arguments
        episode : a key of EPISODES
    Returns
        start, end : the first and the last year of the episode
        change     : the change of each column of `named`, in points of GDP
    """
    start, end = EPISODES[episode]
    # `named.loc[end] - named.loc[start]` subtracts two rows, column by column
    change = named.loc[end] - named.loc[start]
    return start, end, change
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5, U.S. investment, budget deficit and trade deficit
def twin_deficits_chart(episode="1980s: 1979 to 1986"):
    """Investment, the budget deficit and the trade deficit, percent of GDP.

    Draws Fig. 5 (inspired by Fig. 19.5 in Jones), with one episode shaded.

    Arguments
        episode : a key of EPISODES, the episode to shade
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the changes over the episode (episode_change)
    start, end, change = episode_change(episode)

    # Step 2: the four lines; the title reports the changes
    fig = px.line(
        named.reset_index(),
        x="year",
        y=LINES,
        color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, BLUE, GREEN, GRAY],
        labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent of GDP"},
        title=(
            f"{start}→{end}: budget deficit {change['Budget deficit']:+.1f}, "
            f"trade deficit {change['Trade deficit']:+.1f}, "
            f"investment {change['Investment']:+.1f} points"
        ),
    )
    # thick lines, and domestic saving thinner and dotted
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name=LINES[3]), line_width=2, line_dash="dot")

    # Step 3: the zero line, the shaded episode and the axes
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.2, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1958, 2027])
    # room above the lines for the legend
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-5, 28], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25])
    fig.update_layout(
        legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"),
        legend_title_text="",
    )
    return fig
```

[Federal government net saving (`FGDEF`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FGDEF), [Gross domestic product, quarterly (`GDP`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDP),
[Net exports of goods and services (`A019RC1A027NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A019RC1A027NBEA) and [Gross domestic product (`GDPA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA).
Prepared file: [`data/ch19/fig19-5.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/fig19-5.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.5 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- From 1979 to 1986 the budget deficit rose by 2.9 points of GDP and the trade deficit by 2.0 points; investment fell
  by 2.0 points, but it stayed high by historical standards. Foreign saving paid for part of the government's
  borrowing: the first episode of twin deficits.
- From 2000 to 2006 the pattern repeats: the budget deficit rose by 3.2 points and the trade deficit by 2.0 points,
  while investment hardly changed (−0.3).
- In the Great Recession the twins split: the budget deficit soared, investment collapsed, and the trade deficit
  **fell**. In the Covid-19 years the budget deficit jumped by more than 7 points, the trade deficit rose by less than
  1 point, and investment barely moved. Click "Domestic saving" in the legend to hide it; the gap between it and
  investment is the trade deficit.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: decades of twin deficits

We average each line of Fig. 5 over the years of each decade.

```{python}
# The average of each line by decade. `named.index // 10 * 10` turns each year
# into its decade (1987 becomes 1980): `//` divides and drops the remainder.
# `.groupby(...)` then puts the years of each decade together, and `.mean()`
# averages them
decades = named.groupby(named.index // 10 * 10).mean().round(2)
decades.index.name = "decade"
decades
```

Compared with the 1970s, the 1980s had higher budget deficits (4.0 against 3.5 percent of GDP) and much higher trade
deficits (1.75 against 0.18), with **no** fall in investment (18.5 against 18.0). Domestic saving has drifted down,
from about 17 percent of GDP in the 1960s and 1970s to 13–15 percent since 2000, and the trade deficit has filled
the gap.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond the United States: twin deficits in other countries

Did large budget deficits come with large trade deficits elsewhere too? The file `twin_deficits_world.csv` has the
three lines of Fig. 19.5 for most economies, as percent of GDP, from 1980 to 2025:

- `investment`: gross capital formation (World Bank WDI `NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS`). It includes **government** investment,
  so it is higher than the private investment of Fig. 5;
- `budget_deficit`: minus the net lending of the **general government**, federal plus state and local (IMF World
  Economic Outlook, October 2026, `GGXCNL_NGDP`; the last year or two are IMF estimates). For the United States the
  IMF series starts only in 2001;
- `trade_deficit`: minus the WDI trade balance of Figs. 1 and 2.

The same names can hide different definitions, so we first compare the U.S. rows with the BEA data of Fig. 5.

```{python}
# Step 1: load the three lines for most economies, and keep the U.S. rows
twin_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "twin_deficits_world.csv")
us_world = twin_world[twin_world.country == "U.S."].set_index("year")
# Step 2: the U.S. rows next to the BEA data of Fig. 5, in four years
pd.DataFrame({
    "Investment, private (BEA)": named.Investment,
    "Investment, all (WDI)": us_world.investment,
    "Budget deficit, federal (BEA)": named["Budget deficit"],
    "Budget deficit, all governments (IMF)": us_world.budget_deficit,
    "Trade deficit (BEA)": named["Trade deficit"],
    "Trade deficit (WDI)": us_world.trade_deficit,
}).loc[[2007, 2009, 2020, 2024]].round(1)
```

The trade deficits agree within 0.1 point, but total investment is about 4 points higher than private investment,
and the general-government deficit is about 1 point higher than the federal one. `twin_deficits_data` keeps the three
lines of one economy and computes the **correlation** of its two deficits, a number between −1 and +1 that is
positive when they rise and fall together. The figure draws the lines, and its title reports the correlation.

```{python}
# Step 1: readable names for the three lines
WORLD_LINES = {
    "investment": "Investment",
    "budget_deficit": "Budget deficit",
    "trade_deficit": "Trade deficit",
}
# Step 2: the economies with both deficits in at least 5 years, for the menu
counts = twin_world.dropna(subset=["budget_deficit", "trade_deficit"])
counts = counts.groupby("country").year.count()
TWIN_COUNTRIES = sorted(counts[counts >= 5].index)


def twin_deficits_data(country):
    """The three lines of Fig. 5 for one economy, and the correlation of its deficits.

    Fig. 5:  r = the correlation of the budget and the trade deficit

    Arguments
        country : the economy
    Returns
        one  : its rows of `twin_world`, with readable column names
        both : the rows of the years with both deficits
        r    : the correlation of the two deficits, rounded to two decimals
    """
    # Step 1: the economy's rows, and the years that have both deficits
    one = twin_world[twin_world.country == country].rename(columns=WORLD_LINES)
    both = one.dropna(subset=["Budget deficit", "Trade deficit"])
    # Step 2: the correlation of the two columns; + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
    r = round(both["Budget deficit"].corr(both["Trade deficit"]), 2) + 0.0
    return one, both, r
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5 for any economy
def twin_deficits_world(country="U.S."):
    """Investment, the budget deficit and the trade deficit, percent of GDP.

    Draws Fig. 5 (inspired by Fig. 19.5 in Jones) for any economy.

    Arguments
        country : the economy
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data and the correlation (twin_deficits_data)
    one, both, r = twin_deficits_data(country)

    # Step 2: the three lines; the title reports the correlation
    fig = px.line(
        one,
        x="year",
        y=list(WORLD_LINES.values()),
        color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, BLUE, GREEN],
        labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent of GDP"},
        title=(
            f"{country}, {both.year.min()}–{both.year.max()}: correlation of the "
            f"budget and trade deficits {r:+.2f}"
        ),
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)

    # Step 3: the axes. `.stack()` puts all the columns of a table into one long
    # column, so that fit_range sees every value of the three lines
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1975, 2027])         # 1980 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(
        range=fit_range(one[list(WORLD_LINES.values())].stack(), [-5, 28])
    )
    fig.update_layout(
        legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0, y=-0.15, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"),
        legend_title_text="",
    )
    return fig
```

```{python}
for country in ["U.S.", "Germany", "Japan", "Greece", "United Kingdom", "Australia"]:
```

In the general-government data since 2001, the two U.S. deficits are **negatively** correlated (−0.36): the largest
budget deficits came in the recessions of 2009 and 2020, when the trade deficit shrank. Twin deficits are clearer
in Germany (+0.57) and Greece (+0.56), where both deficits rose together before the euro crisis and fell
together after it. Over long periods the "twins" are only loosely related: what matters is what happens to private
saving and investment at the same time.

## Net foreign assets and foreign debt

Years of trade deficits add up to a debt to the rest of the world. We measure that debt for the United States and for every other economy.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 6: Net international investment position of the United States

**Goal.** Follow how decades of trade deficits turned the United States from a lender into a debtor.

The **net international investment position** (NIIP) is what U.S. residents own abroad (foreign shares, bonds,
factories) minus what foreigners own in the United States, at the end of each year. When it is negative, it is the
**net foreign debt**. Each year's trade deficit is new borrowing, so the position should fall by about the size of
the deficit. With our function `accumulate`, we start from the 1976 position and add the trade balance of every later
year, as in the Oddtopia table. We also compare the current data with the same series as published in July 2023,
which the textbook used.

```{python}
# Step 1: three versions of the position, percent of GDP: the current data, the
# data of July 2023, and the 1976 position plus the sum of the later trade
# balances (accumulate, equation (5) with r-bar = 0)
niip = pd.DataFrame({
    "Current data": share_of_gdp(us.niip, us.gdp),
    "As published in July 2023 (the textbook)": share_of_gdp(
        us.niip_2023, us.gdp_2023
    ),
    "1976 position + sum of later trade balances": share_of_gdp(
        accumulate(us.niip[1976], us.net_exports.loc[1977:]), us.gdp
    ),
})

# Step 2: the check against the figure's data file: the largest gap, in points
check = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig19-6.csv").set_index("year")
print(
    "Largest difference from fig19-6.csv: "
    f"{(niip['Current data'] - check.niip_pct_gdp).abs().max():.4f} points"
)
niip.loc[[1980, 1988, 1989, 2008, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2025]].round(1)
```

For the chart we stack the three series into one column, and we keep the current data without the
years before 1976.

```{python}
# Step 1: the long shape for the chart: one row per year and series
long = niip.reset_index().melt(
    id_vars="year",
    var_name="Series",
    value_name="Percent of GDP",
).dropna()
# Step 2: the current data, from 1976 on
current = niip["Current data"].dropna()
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 6, the three lines
# Step 1: one line per series; the title reports the first year as a net debtor
# and the latest net foreign debt
fig = px.line(
    long,
    x="year",
    y="Percent of GDP",
    color="Series",
    color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GRAY, TEAL],
    labels={"year": "Year"},
    title=(
        f"The U.S. turned net debtor in {current[current < 0].index.min()}; "
        f"its net foreign debt was {-current.iloc[-1]:.1f}% of GDP "
        f"in {current.index[-1]}"
    ),
)
```

**Sources.** Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), International Investment Position and National Income
and Product Accounts, via FRED: [U.S. net international investment position (`IIPUSNETIA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IIPUSNETIA),
[Gross domestic product (`GDPA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA) and
[Net exports of goods and services (`A019RC1A027NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A019RC1A027NBEA); the July 2023 vintages of
[`IIPUSNETIA`](https://alfred.stlouisfed.org/series?seid=IIPUSNETIA) and
[`GDPA`](https://alfred.stlouisfed.org/series?seid=GDPA) via ALFRED.
Prepared file: [`data/ch19/us_trade.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/us_trade.csv), checked against [`data/ch19/fig19-6.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/fig19-6.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.6 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- Until 1988 the United States was a **net creditor**: it owned more abroad than foreigners owned in the United
  States. Since 1989 it has been a **net debtor**, and its net foreign debt has grown to about 70 percent of GDP.
- The dotted line adds up the trade balances since 1976. It has the same downward trend: the foreign debt is,
  roughly, the sum of past trade deficits. But the gap between the two lines is large in some years (37 points of
  GDP in 2010), because the position also changes when asset prices and the dollar move, and with the income earned
  on foreign assets. Until 2020 these effects kept the debt below the summed deficits; in 2021 and since 2023 it is above them.
- The textbook's data (dashed) show a trough of about −80 percent in 2021. BEA has since revised the series: the
  current data are 9 to 16 points of GDP less negative for 2020–2022, and the deepest point is now 2024.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: the foreign debt

The textbook says that the United States was a net creditor "up until the late 1980s" and that its net foreign debt
"exceeded 60 percent of GDP in 2022".

```{python}
# Step 1: the last year as a net creditor, and 2022 in both vintages
july_2023 = niip["As published in July 2023 (the textbook)"].dropna()
print(f"Last year as a net creditor: {current[current > 0].index.max()}")
print(
    f"2022: {current[2022]:.1f}% of GDP in current data, "
    f"{july_2023[2022]:.1f}% as published in July 2023"
)

# Step 2: the years with a debt above 60 percent of GDP, and the revision to
# 2021, in trillions of dollars (the data are in billions)
print(f"Years below -60% of GDP in current data: {list(current[current < -60].index)}")
print(
    "Revision to the 2021 position: "
    f"{(us.niip[2021] - us.niip_2023[2021]) / 1000:+.2f} trillion dollars"
)

# Step 3: the change in the position from 1976 to 2025, and the sum of the trade
# balances of 1977 to 2025
change, summed = us.niip[2025] - us.niip[1976], us.net_exports.loc[1977:2025].sum()
print(
    f"1976 to 2025: position {change / 1000:+.1f} trillion dollars; "
    f"sum of trade balances {summed / 1000:+.1f} trillion"
)
```

In the textbook's vintage the net foreign debt was 63.5 percent of GDP in 2022, as the text says. In the current data
it is 54.6 percent for 2022, because BEA has revised the position upward by 1.9 to 3.4 trillion dollars for
2020–2022. The statement still holds for the most recent years: the debt is above 60 percent of GDP in 2021 and in
2023–2025. Over the whole period, trade deficits of 18.0 trillion dollars came with a fall of 22.0 trillion in the
investment position.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond the United States: creditors and debtors around the world

The BEA measures only the U.S. position. For other countries, economists use the **External Wealth of Nations**
database of Philip Lane and Gian Maria Milesi-Ferretti (Brookings, release of February 2026), which collects and
completes the official investment positions of about 200 economies. The file `niip_world.csv` has the net position
(foreign assets minus foreign liabilities, gold included) as a percent of GDP, both in US dollars, at the end of each
year from 1970 to 2024. First we check its U.S. rows against the BEA data of the figure above.

```{python}
# Step 1: load the net position of every economy, percent of GDP
niip_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "niip_world.csv")
ewn_us = niip_world[niip_world.country == "U.S."].set_index("year").niip
# Step 2: the U.S. position in three sources, side by side
pd.DataFrame({
    "BEA, current": current,
    "BEA, July 2023": july_2023,
    "External Wealth of Nations": ewn_us,
}).loc[[2010, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024]].round(1)
```

**Look at your data.** Up to 2019 the two sources agree to the decimal, because the database copies the BEA. From 2020
on it keeps BEA numbers from **before** the later revisions (its 2020–2022 values are close to the July 2023
vintage), so its U.S. position is 7 to 15 points of GDP more negative than the current BEA data: −90.6 percent
instead of −75.3 in 2024. When you combine sources, check that they measure the same thing at the same vintage.

`niip_world_data` keeps the rows of the chosen economies and finds each one's latest position, which the
title of the figure reports.

```{python}
def niip_world_data(countries):
    """The data of Fig. 6 for any economies, and the latest position of each.

    The net international investment position: foreign assets minus foreign
    liabilities, percent of GDP (External Wealth of Nations).

    Arguments
        countries : the economies to show
    Returns
        rows   : the chosen economies' rows of `niip_world`
        latest : each economy's position in its latest year, percent of GDP
    """
    rows = niip_world[niip_world.country.isin(countries)]
    # each economy's last row: its latest year
    latest = rows.groupby("country").last().niip
    return rows, latest
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 6 for any economies
def niip_world_chart(countries=("U.S.",)):
    """The net international investment position, percent of GDP, of any economies.

    Draws Fig. 6 (inspired by Fig. 19.6 in Jones) for any list of economies.

    Arguments
        countries : the economies to show
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (niip_world_data)
    rows, latest = niip_world_data(countries)
    if len(rows) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Choose at least one economy"))

    # Step 2: the title names two economies, in whole percent (+ 0 turns -0
    # into 0), and counts the rest
    names = []
    for name in latest.index[:2]:
        names.append(f"{name} {round(latest[name]) + 0:+d}%")
    more = f" + {len(latest) - 2} more" if len(latest) > 2 else ""

    # Step 3: one line per economy, in its own color
    fig = px.line(
        rows,
        x="year",
        y="niip",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        labels={"year": "Year", "niip": "Percent of GDP"},
        title="Latest net foreign assets, % of GDP: " + ", ".join(names) + more,
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)

    # Step 4: the axes: the textbook's range when the data fit in it
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1965, 2027])         # 1970 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(rows.niip, [-100, 30]))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

**Sources.** Data: Philip R. Lane and Gian Maria Milesi-Ferretti,
[External Wealth of Nations database](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-external-wealth-of-nations-database/),
Brookings release of February 2026 (Lane and Milesi-Ferretti 2018, *IMF Economic Review*); World Bank, [country and lending groups](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups) (regions and income groups of the menus).

## Concluding remarks

- Trade has become much more important: U.S. exports and imports have risen from about 4 percent of GDP each in 1950
  to 11 and 14 percent. Since 1976 imports have exceeded exports every year, and the trade deficit reached 5.7 percent
  of GDP in 2006.
- The national income identity shows what a deficit means. With $NX < 0$, a country uses more than it produces
  (equation 1), and it invests more than it saves, $NX = S - I$ (equation 4). The deficit is borrowing from the
  rest of the world, and past deficits add up to the **net foreign debt** (equation 5), about 70 percent of U.S. GDP
  today. In present value, trade has to balance over time (equation 6), and a steady deficit leads to a stable debt
  ratio only if GDP grows faster than the return on the debt (equation 7).
- Trade can make everyone better off: across time it shares risks (Oddtopia and Eventopia), and across goods it lets
  countries specialize by **comparative advantage**. In the North–South model the world price of equation (10)
  lies between the two autarky prices of equation (9), condition (11), and each country gains in the good it imports.
  Free migration follows **absolute** advantage and raises world output even more.
- The data hold surprises: the textbook's fast-growing economies run surpluses, not deficits, and the large U.S.
  budget deficits of the 1980s and 2000s came with large trade deficits (the **twin deficits**). Looking beyond the
  textbook's countries changes both stories: across all economies, faster growth goes with slightly smaller trade
  balances, and the twin deficits are clear in some countries (Germany, Greece) but not in others.
- The data also teach care: the textbook's "2019" bars are 2017 data, revisions changed the recent U.S. foreign debt
  by up to 16 points of GDP, and two sources for the same country can differ by vintage and definition.
- The next chapter, **exchange rates and international finance**, brings trade into the short-run model and asks how
  the exchange rate adjusts.
