**Problem 1 (Basic): Japan's trade deficits after Fukushima.** After the Fukushima nuclear accident of 2011, Japan
took all of its nuclear reactors offline for safety checks, and its power companies had to import large amounts of
liquefied natural gas instead ([U.S. Energy Information Administration](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=38533)).
In the World Bank data of Fig. 2, Japan's trade balance turned negative for five years. Its current account, however,
stayed positive ([IMF, World Economic Outlook, current account balance](https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/BCA_NGDPD@WEO/JPN)):

| | 2011 | 2012 | 2013 | 2014 | 2015 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade balance, % of GDP (World Bank) | −0.64 | −1.63 | −2.38 | −2.55 | −0.54 |
| Current account, % of GDP (IMF) | 2.1 | 0.9 | 0.9 | 0.7 | 3.0 |

(a) The Model overview defines the current account as $CA_t = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1}$. Use it to compute Japan's net
income from its foreign assets in each year, in percent of GDP.

(b) At the end of 2010, Japan's net foreign assets were 54.7 percent of GDP (the
[External Wealth of Nations](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-external-wealth-of-nations-database/) data of
Fig. 6). What average return $\bar{r}$ does your number for 2011 imply? Ignore the growth of GDP.

(c) By the end of 2015, Japan's net foreign assets had risen to 61.1 percent of GDP. How can a country run trade
deficits for five years and still end up a bigger creditor? Answer with equation (5).

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

The income from foreign assets is the gap between the current account and the trade balance. For (b), divide that
income by the assets held at the start of the year. For (c), write equation (5) as
$F_t - F_{t-1} = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1}$: which flow changes the stock of assets, the trade balance or the current
account?

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Solve the definition for the income term, $\bar{r}F_{t-1} = CA_t - NX_t$. In percent of GDP:

| | 2011 | 2012 | 2013 | 2014 | 2015 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $CA - NX$ | $2.1 + 0.64 = 2.74$ | $0.9 + 1.63 = 2.53$ | $0.9 + 2.38 = 3.28$ | $0.7 + 2.55 = 3.25$ | $3.0 + 0.54 = 3.54$ |

On average Japan earned about 3.1 percent of GDP a year from abroad, more than enough to pay for its trade deficits.
(The data's current account also counts transfers such as aid and remittances, which the model leaves out, so these
gaps are the income from foreign assets plus net transfers.)

**(b)** Divide the income by the assets at the start of the year:

$$\bar{r} \approx \frac{\bar{r}F_{2010}}{F_{2010}} = \frac{2.74}{54.7} = 0.050,$$

a return of about 5 percent a year. That is high for a safe investment. The reason is that the income is earned on
gross positions, which are much larger than the net one: if what Japan owns abroad earns more than what it owes
foreigners costs, the return on the *net* position looks high.

**(c)** Equation (5) says $F_t - F_{t-1} = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1} = CA_t$: net foreign assets grow by the
**current account**, not by the trade balance. From 2011 to 2015 Japan's trade balances add up to
$-0.64 - 1.63 - 2.38 - 2.55 - 0.54 = -7.74$ percent of a year's GDP, but its current accounts add up to
$2.1 + 0.9 + 0.9 + 0.7 + 3.0 = 7.6$ percent, so its claims on the rest of the world kept growing. The data show a rise
of $61.1 - 54.7 = 6.4$ points; the rest of the difference comes from changes in asset prices, in the yen and in GDP.
A creditor can run trade deficits for as long as they are smaller than its income from abroad. A debtor is in the
opposite position: its interest payments make its current account weaker than its trade balance.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 2 (Intermediate): Norway's oil fund and the spend-only-the-return rule.** Norway puts its government's oil
and gas revenue into the Government Pension Fund Global, which invests abroad. A fiscal rule says that, over time,
the government may spend only the fund's expected real return, now estimated at 3 percent a year, and never its
capital. At the end of 2025 the fund was worth about NOK 21,300 billion, almost four times Norway's GDP
([norskpetroleum.no](https://www.norskpetroleum.no/en/economy/management-of-revenues/), run by Norway's Ministry of
Energy and its Offshore Directorate). In our data, Norway's net foreign assets were 358 percent of GDP at the end of
2024 (the file of Fig. 6), and its trade surplus averaged 12.2 percent of GDP from 2000 to 2024 (the file of Fig. 2).

Take a stylized Norway whose foreign assets $F$ earn a real return of $\bar{r} = 0.03$.

(a) Suppose that, once the oil runs out, Norway runs a trade deficit equal to the return on its assets in every year,
$NX_t = -\bar{r}F_{t-1}$. Show with equation (5) that its foreign assets then never change. What is its current
account?

(b) Show that this plan satisfies the intertemporal budget constraint, equation (6), for a creditor with $F_0 > 0$,
as the horizon $T$ goes to infinity. You may use $\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} 1/(1+\bar{r})^t = 1/\bar{r}$.

(c) Now measure the assets relative to GDP, $f = F/Y = 3.58$. With no growth of GDP, how large a trade deficit, in
percent of GDP, does the rule allow? With real GDP growth of $\bar{g} = 0.02$, which constant trade balance keeps
$f$ at 3.58? Why does growth lower the deficit that Norway can afford?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

For (a), put the trade balance into $F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} + NX_t$. For (b), take the constant $\bar{r}F_0$ out
of the sum. For (c), use the ratio form of equation (5) from the Model overview,
$f_t = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f_{t-1} + nx_t$, set $f_t = f_{t-1}$ and solve for $nx$. A real return
together with real growth is fine here: the ratio $F/Y$ is the same in real and in nominal terms.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Substitute $NX_t = -\bar{r}F_{t-1}$ into equation (5):

$$F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} - \bar{r}F_{t-1} = F_{t-1}.$$

The assets stay at $F_0$ forever. The current account is $CA_t = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1} = -\bar{r}F_{t-1} +
\bar{r}F_{t-1} = 0$: the return pays for the extra imports, and nothing is added to or taken from the fund.

**(b)** With $NX_t = -\bar{r}F_0$ in every year,

$$\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = -\bar{r}F_0\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1 + \bar{r})^t}
= -\bar{r}F_0 \times \frac{1}{\bar{r}} = -F_0,$$

which is equation (6). The end term of the derivation also vanishes, as it must: $F_T/(1 + \bar{r})^T =
F_0/(1 + \bar{r})^T$ goes to zero as $T$ grows. For a creditor, equation (6) reads the other way round than for a
debtor: the present value of its trade balances is *negative*, so it can run trade deficits forever.

**(c)** With no growth, $nx = -\bar{r}f = -0.03 \times 3.58 = -0.107$: a deficit of 10.7 percent of GDP in every
year. With growth, setting $f_t = f_{t-1} = f$ gives

$$f = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f + nx \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
nx = f\left(1 - \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\right) = -\frac{(\bar{r} - \bar{g})\,f}{1 + \bar{g}}
= -\frac{0.01 \times 3.58}{1.02} = -0.035.$$

The rule now allows a deficit of only 3.5 percent of GDP. The return is worth $0.03 \times 3.58/1.02 = 0.105$, or
10.5 percent of this year's GDP, but $0.02 \times 3.58/1.02 = 0.070$, or 7.0 points of it, must be invested abroad
again, so that the fund keeps up with a growing economy. Today Norway is still far from that stage: it runs trade
surpluses (12.2 percent of GDP on average since 2000), because each year it turns more oil and gas into foreign assets.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 3 (Challenge): Can tariffs close the trade deficit?** In April 2025 the United States put new tariffs on
imports from its trading partners, by an executive order whose title names "large and persistent annual United States
goods trade deficits" as the problem to fix
([Executive Order 14257, Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/04/07/2025-06063/regulating-imports-with-a-reciprocal-tariff-to-rectify-trade-practices-that-contribute-to-large-and)).
Customs duties collected rose from 84 billion dollars in 2024 to 269 billion in 2025, or from 0.284 to 0.871 percent
of GDP ([BEA, Customs duties (`B235RC1Q027SBEA`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/B235RC1Q027SBEA),
annual averages of the quarterly data). The file of Fig. 5 shows the other terms of the identity, in percent of GDP:

| | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Trade deficit | 3.000 | 2.985 |
| Federal budget deficit | 6.474 | 5.761 |
| Private investment | 18.060 | 18.007 |

(a) Write the trade balance as in Step 5 of the saving–investment block, $NX = (Y - T - C - I) + (T - G)$. Suppose
the extra customs revenue had raised government saving $T - G$ one for one, while private saving and investment
stayed the same. By how much would the trade deficit have fallen?

(b) Now use the table. By how much did private saving minus investment, $Y - T - C - I$, change from 2024 to 2025,
according to the identity? What does that imply for private saving itself? (The budget deficit here is the federal
one, so treat state and local governments as part of the private term.)

(c) Many economists argue that a tariff can lower the trade deficit only if it raises national saving or lowers
investment. Explain this argument with equation (4). Give two reasons why private saving might fall when tariffs
rise. Is one year of data enough to judge the policy?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

For (a), the change in customs revenue, in points of GDP, goes one for one into $NX$. For (b), solve the identity for
the private term, $Y - T - C - I = NX - (T - G) = \text{budget deficit} - \text{trade deficit}$, compute it for both
years, and add back the change in investment. For (c), think about who pays a tariff and how they react, and recall
that $NX = EX - IM$: if $S - I$ does not move, what must happen to exports when imports fall?

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Customs duties rose by $0.871 - 0.284 = 0.587$, about 0.59 points of GDP. With the private term fixed,
$\Delta NX = \Delta(T - G) = +0.59$, so the trade deficit would have fallen from 3.00 to about 2.41 percent of GDP.

**(b)** The private term is the budget deficit minus the trade deficit:

$$2024:\; 6.474 - 3.000 = 3.474, \qquad 2025:\; 5.761 - 2.985 = 2.776, \qquad \text{change} = -0.698.$$

Private saving minus investment fell by about 0.70 points of GDP. Investment changed by $18.007 - 18.060 = -0.053$, so
private saving itself fell by about $0.698 + 0.053 = 0.75$ points. In 2025 the federal government saved more (its
deficit fell by 0.71 points, in part thanks to the tariffs), the private sector saved less by about the same amount,
and the trade deficit hardly moved.

**(c)** Equation (4), $NX = S - I$, holds whatever the tariff. Tariffs make imports dearer and may reduce them, but if
national saving and investment do not change, net exports cannot change either: exports must then fall by about as
much as imports. Possible channels are retaliation by other countries, a stronger dollar (Chapter 20), and imported
parts that make U.S. exports dearer. Two reasons why private saving may fall:

1. A tariff is a tax, paid by importers and, through higher prices, by households. If households keep their
   consumption smooth (Chapter 16), they pay it by saving less, and the rise in government saving is then offset one
   for one.
2. Firms that absorb part of the tariff earn smaller profits, so business saving falls.

One year is not enough to judge. Many things change at once, and the timing of trade was distorted: in the first
quarter of 2025, net exports fell to −1,215 billion dollars at an annual rate, from −944 billion in the last quarter of
2024 ([BEA, Net exports of goods and services (`NETEXP`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NETEXP)), a
jump that suggests importers bought ahead of the tariffs. A fair test compares several years with what saving and
investment would have done without the tariffs.

</details>

**Problem 4 (Basic): Mexico's opening after NAFTA.** The North American Free Trade Agreement between Canada, Mexico
and the United States entered into force on January 1, 1994, and its tariff cuts were phased in until 2008
([Office of the U.S. Trade Representative](https://ustr.gov/about-us/policy-offices/press-office/ustr-archives/north-american-free-trade-agreement-nafta)).
Use the World Bank's World Development Indicators,
[exports](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS) and
[imports](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS) of goods and services in percent of GDP, in the file
`wdi_trade.csv` of Fig. 1.

(a) Compute Mexico's openness, exports plus imports in percent of GDP, in 1993 and in 2024. By what factor did it
grow?

(b) In which year was Mexico's openness highest, and how high was it?

(c) Compute the openness of Canada and of the United States in 1993 and in 2024. Which of the three economies is the
most open today?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Read the file with `trade = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")` and keep one country with
`trade[trade.country == "Mexico"].set_index("year")`. The sum of its `exports` and `imports` columns is a Series with
the years as labels: `.loc[[1993, 2024]]` picks two years, and `.idxmax()` gives the year of the largest value. A loop
over `["Canada", "U.S."]` repeats the steps for the other two.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Add the two shares, pick the years, and repeat for the neighbors:

```python
trade = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")
mexico = trade[trade.country == "Mexico"].set_index("year")
open_mexico = mexico.exports + mexico.imports
print(open_mexico.loc[[1993, 2024]].round(1).to_dict())
print(f"Growth factor: {open_mexico[2024] / open_mexico[1993]:.1f}")
print(f"Highest: {open_mexico.max():.1f}% of GDP in {open_mexico.idxmax()}")
for name in ["Canada", "U.S."]:
    one = trade[trade.country == name].set_index("year")
    print(name, (one.exports + one.imports).loc[[1993, 2024]].round(1).to_dict())
```

It prints `{1993: 26.2, 2024: 75.4}`, a growth factor of 2.9, a peak of 88.8 percent of GDP in 2022, then
`Canada {1993: 58.2, 2024: 65.1}` and `U.S. {1993: 20.0, 2024: 25.0}`.

Mexico's openness almost tripled, and Mexico is now the most open of the three economies. Canada was already open in
1993 (it had had a free trade agreement with the United States since 1989, as the USTR page explains), and the United
States remains one of the least open economies in the world. A word of caution: Mexico's openness jumped by 14.5
points from 1994 to 1995 (from 29.15 to 43.67 percent of GDP), far faster than tariff cuts phased in over 14 years
could explain. Other forces move these shares too, such as the exchange rate (Chapter 20). The data show that Mexico
opened up after NAFTA; by themselves they do not tell how much of the opening NAFTA caused.

</details>

**Problem 5 (Intermediate): Do large economies trade less?** After Fig. 1 we found the United States among the least
open economies, and suggested that large economies trade less because much of their trade takes place inside their
own borders. Test this for 2023 with two measures of size from
[Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) (file `pwt_trade_world.csv`): GDP at PPP
(`cgdpo`) and population (`pop`). Openness is exports plus imports in percent of GDP, from the World Bank file
`wdi_trade.csv`.

(a) Merge the 2023 rows of the two files by their country code `iso3`. How many economies have openness, GDP and
population?

(b) Compute the correlation of the log of openness with the log of GDP, and with the log of population. Which measure
of size goes with openness more closely? Why might that be?

(c) Among the 15 most populous economies, what is the median openness, and how does it compare with the median of all
economies? Which of the 15 is the big exception?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

`a.merge(b, on="iso3")` joins two tables row by row where the codes match, and `.dropna(subset=[...])` drops the
economies with a missing value. `np.log` takes the log of a whole column, and `x.corr(y)` gives a correlation. For
(c), `.sort_values("pop", ascending=False).head(15)` keeps the 15 largest, and `.median()` gives the middle value.
Write the population column as `["pop"]`, because `.pop` is also the name of a pandas method. For the "why", think of
Singapore and Ireland.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Make openness in the World Bank file, merge, take logs, then sort by population:

```python
trade = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")
size = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_trade_world.csv")
open_2023 = trade[trade.year == 2023].copy()
open_2023["openness"] = open_2023.exports + open_2023.imports
size_2023 = size[size.year == 2023][["iso3", "cgdpo", "pop"]]
merged = open_2023.merge(size_2023, on="iso3").dropna(subset=["openness", "cgdpo", "pop"])
print(f"{len(merged)} economies")
log_open = np.log(merged.openness)
print(f"Correlation with log GDP: {log_open.corr(np.log(merged.cgdpo)):.2f}")
print(f"Correlation with log population: {log_open.corr(np.log(merged['pop'])):.2f}")
largest = merged.sort_values("pop", ascending=False).head(15)
print(f"Median openness: {largest.openness.median():.1f}% for the 15 most populous, {merged.openness.median():.1f}% for all")
print(largest[["country", "pop", "openness"]].round(1).to_string(index=False))
```

It prints 156 economies, correlations of −0.18 with log GDP and −0.50 with log population, and medians of 41.3 percent
for the 15 most populous economies against 79.0 percent for all of them. In the list, every large economy but one has
an openness between 20.6 percent (Ethiopia) and 86.7 percent (DR Congo); the United States, at 24.9 percent, is the
second lowest.

The claim holds, and it holds much more clearly for population than for GDP. GDP mixes two things: the number of
people, which sets how much trade can take place inside the borders, and income per person, which has little to do
with that. Several small, rich economies are trading hubs with extreme openness, such as Singapore (about 324
percent) and Ireland (about 240 percent) in 2023, and they blur the link between GDP and openness. The big exception
among the 15 is **Vietnam**: with 100.4 million people, its openness is 165.0 percent, because its exports alone were
86.7 percent of GDP. Size makes trade less likely to be large, but it does not rule it out.

</details>

**Problem 6 (Challenge): Who borrowed abroad before the euro crisis?** Step 5 of the saving–investment block splits
the trade balance into a private and a public part, $NX = (Y - T - C - I) + (T - G)$. With both deficits in percent of
GDP, the private part, private saving minus investment, is therefore the budget deficit minus the trade deficit. The
file `twin_deficits_world.csv` of Fig. 5 has both deficits for most economies: the general-government budget deficit
from the [IMF World Economic Outlook](https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/GGXCNL_NGDP) and the trade deficit
from the [World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.RSB.GNFS.ZS).

(a) Compute private saving minus investment for Greece, Portugal and Spain in 2007, just before the crisis, and in
2013.

(b) In 2007, in which country was the trade deficit the "twin" of a large budget deficit, and in which did it come
mostly from private borrowing?

(c) The European Union's rules set a reference value of 3 percent of GDP for government deficits
([EUR-Lex, the excessive deficit procedure](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=LEGISSUM:l25020)).
Would a strict 3 percent rule have prevented these three trade deficits of 2007? What does your answer suggest about
the numbers that policymakers should watch?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Keep the three countries and the two years with `.isin([...])`, combining the two tests with `&`, and add a column
`budget_deficit - trade_deficit`. A negative private part means that households and firms invested more than they
saved, and borrowed the difference from abroad. In this file the budget deficit includes government investment, so
the private part is private saving minus *private* investment.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Keep the six rows and compute the private part from the identity:

```python
deficits = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "twin_deficits_world.csv")
keep = deficits.country.isin(["Greece", "Portugal", "Spain"]) & deficits.year.isin([2007, 2013])
euro = deficits[keep].copy()
euro["private"] = euro.budget_deficit - euro.trade_deficit      # private saving minus investment
columns = ["country", "year", "budget_deficit", "trade_deficit", "private", "investment"]
print(euro[columns].sort_values(["country", "year"]).round(1).to_string(index=False))
```

| | budget deficit | trade deficit | private saving minus investment | investment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Greece 2007 | 6.8 | 11.0 | −4.2 | 26.7 |
| Greece 2013 | 4.1 | 2.3 | 1.8 | 12.1 |
| Portugal 2007 | 2.9 | 7.6 | −4.7 | 23.1 |
| Portugal 2013 | 5.2 | −1.1 | 6.3 | 14.7 |
| Spain 2007 | −1.9 | 5.8 | −7.7 | 30.5 |
| Spain 2013 | 7.5 | −3.8 | 11.3 | 17.4 |

**(b)** Greece had twin deficits: of its trade deficit of 11.0 percent of GDP, 6.8 points came from the government and
4.2 from the private sector. Spain's government ran a **surplus** of 1.9 percent of GDP, so its whole trade deficit,
and more, was private borrowing (7.7 points), at a time when investment was 30.5 percent of GDP. In Portugal, private
borrowing (4.7 points) was larger than the budget deficit (2.9 percent of GDP).

**(c)** No. Spain and Portugal respected the 3 percent reference value in 2007 and still had trade deficits of 5.8 and
7.6 percent of GDP; only Greece broke the rule. A fiscal rule watches only the second term of the identity, and the
private term can be just as large. By 2013 the private sectors had swung to surpluses (Spain by
$11.3 - (-7.7) = 19.0$ points), mostly because investment collapsed, and the trade deficits had shrunk or turned
into surpluses (Greece from 11.0 to 2.3 percent of GDP, Spain from a deficit of 5.8 to a surplus of 3.8). So
policymakers should also watch the trade or current-account balance and private borrowing.
Since the crisis, the EU also runs a
[Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure](https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/economic-and-fiscal-governance/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure_en)
that aims to spot and correct harmful imbalances of this kind.

</details>

### Modeling problems

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 7 (Basic): Paying for a hurricane.** A hypothetical island economy is hit by a hurricane. To rebuild, it
runs trade deficits of 5 percent of GDP for 3 years, borrowing abroad at the interest rate $\bar{r}$, and then repays
with equal trade surpluses over the next 10 years. It has no foreign assets before the storm, $F_0 = 0$, and its GDP
stays constant, so everything can be measured in percent of GDP. The calculator below applies equation (5) year by
year and picks the surplus that satisfies equation (6). Answer with its sliders.

(a) If the loans are free of interest, $\bar{r} = 0$, how large must each surplus be? Check it with equation (6).

(b) If the island borrows at a market rate of 4 percent, how large is each surplus, and how large is the debt when the
rebuilding ends?

(c) A development bank offers a loan at 1 percent instead. How much smaller is each year's surplus than at 4 percent,
and how much less does the island hand over in total during the 10 years?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Read the title of the calculator for each interest rate. To check by hand: with $\bar{r} = 0$, equation (6) says that
the trade balances add up to zero. With $\bar{r} > 0$, find the debt after the 3 years of deficits with equation (5),
then pick the surplus $S$ whose present value over 10 years equals that debt:
$S\sum_{j=1}^{10} 1/(1+\bar{r})^j = \text{debt}$.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def repayment_plan(deficit=5.0, years=3, r=0.0, repay_years=10):
    """Equations (5) and (6): trade deficits for some years, then equal surpluses that repay the debt (% of GDP)."""
    pv = 0.0
    for j in range(1, repay_years + 1):
        pv = pv + 1 / (1 + r / 100) ** j                       # present value of 1 a year (Appendix C.12)
    F, flows, assets = 0.0, [], []
    for t in range(1, years + repay_years + 1):
        nx = -deficit if t <= years else -assets[years - 1] / pv   # equation (6): the surpluses repay the debt
        F = (1 + r / 100) * F + nx                             # equation (5)
        flows.append(nx)
        assets.append(F)
    year = list(range(1, years + repay_years + 1))
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=year, y=flows, name="Trade balance, NX", marker_color=TEAL))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=year, y=assets, mode="lines+markers", name="Net foreign assets, F",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Surplus needed: {flows[-1]:.2f}% of GDP a year; peak debt {-assets[years - 1]:.1f}% of GDP",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Years after the storm", range=[0.3, 15.7]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Percent of GDP", range=[-60, 12]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.03, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))
    return fig


interact(repayment_plan,
         deficit=FloatSlider(value=5.0, min=1.0, max=10.0, step=1.0, description="deficit, % of GDP", style=WIDE),
         years=IntSlider(value=3, min=1, max=5, step=1, description="years of deficits", style=WIDE),
         r=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="interest rate r, %", style=WIDE),
         repay_years=fixed(10));
```

**Source.** A calculator built on the accounting for net foreign assets in the Model overview, equations (5) and (6), adapted from the discussion of trade across time in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** With $\bar{r} = 0$ the island owes $3 \times 5 = 15$ percent of GDP after the rebuilding, and equation (6)
with $F_0 = 0$ says that the trade balances must add up to zero: $3 \times (-5) + 10\,S = 0$, so $S = 1.5$ percent of
GDP a year. The calculator's title reads "Surplus needed: 1.50% of GDP a year; peak debt 15.0% of GDP".

**(b)** With interest, the debt grows during the rebuilding. By equation (5), the debt after 3 years is

$$5\,(1.04)^2 + 5\,(1.04) + 5 = 15.61$$

percent of GDP. The surplus must have a present value equal to that debt: $S \times 8.111 = 15.61$, where
$8.111 = \sum_{j=1}^{10} 1/1.04^j$, so $S = 1.92$ percent of GDP a year.

**(c)** At 1 percent the debt is 15.15 percent of GDP and the surplus 1.60 percent a year, 0.32 points less than at 4
percent. Over 10 years the island hands over 16.00 percent of a year's GDP instead of 19.24 percent: the cheaper loan
saves it about 3.2 percent of a year's output. The code below confirms the numbers:

```python
for rate in [0.0, 0.04, 0.01]:
    debt, pv = 0.0, 0.0
    for k in range(3):
        debt = (1 + rate) * debt + 5                     # equation (5), for the debt
    for j in range(1, 11):
        pv = pv + 1 / (1 + rate) ** j
    surplus = debt / pv                                  # equation (6)
    print(f"r = {rate:.0%}: debt {debt:.2f}% of GDP, surplus {surplus:.2f}% a year, {10 * surplus:.2f}% in total")
print(repayment_plan(5.0, 3, 4.0, 10).layout.title.text)
```

It prints `r = 0%: debt 15.00% of GDP, surplus 1.50% a year, 15.00% in total`, then 15.61, 1.92 and 19.24 for 4
percent, 15.15, 1.60 and 16.00 for 1 percent, and the calculator's title for 4 percent. The lesson of equation (6) is
that every deficit is repaid by later surpluses; the interest rate decides how large they must be.

</details>

**Problem 8 (Intermediate): How much foreign debt can the United States carry?** The net foreign debt of the United
States was 70.9 percent of GDP at the end of 2025 (Fig. 6), and its trade deficit has been about 3 percent of GDP for
years. The calculator starts from the 2025 position and applies the ratio form of equation (5),
$f_t = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f_{t-1} + nx$, for 100 years with a constant trade balance. The dashed line
is the long-run ratio $f^*$ of equation (7). Here $\bar{g}$ is the growth rate of nominal GDP and $\bar{r}$ the net
return that foreigners earn on the debt. Answer with the sliders.

(a) With $nx = -3$, $\bar{g} = 4$ and $\bar{r} = 0$ percent, does the debt ratio rise or fall from its 2025 level, and
where does it settle? Which constant trade balance would hold the ratio at its 2025 level?

(b) A policy committee wants the net foreign debt never to exceed 100 percent of GDP in the long run, even if
foreigners earn a net return of 2 percent on it while nominal GDP grows at 4 percent. What is the largest steady
trade deficit that meets this goal? Find it roughly with the sliders, then exactly with equation (7).

(c) Suppose instead that nominal growth slows to 3 percent, the return is 2 percent, and the deficit stays at 3
percent of GDP. Where does the ratio head, and in which year does the debt pass 100 percent of GDP? Why does a small
change in $\bar{g} - \bar{r}$ matter so much?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

The title shows $f^*$ and the year in which the debt passes 100 percent of GDP. For the trade balance that holds a
ratio $f$, solve equation (7) for $nx$: $nx = f\,(\bar{g} - \bar{r})/(1 + \bar{g})$. For (c), compare the factor
$\frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}$ in the cases, and look at the denominator of equation (7).

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def debt_projection(nx=-3.0, g=4.0, r=0.0):
    """Equations (5) and (7): U.S. net foreign assets (% of GDP) if the trade balance stays at nx after 2025."""
    history = share_of_gdp(us.niip, us.gdp).dropna()                   # the BEA data of Fig. 6
    f_star = round(100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(nx / 100, g / 100, r / 100), 1) + 0.0    # equation (7)
    passed = "never above 100% of GDP" if f_star >= -100 else "above 100% of GDP only after 2125"
    ratio, path, years = history.iloc[-1] / 100, [], list(range(history.index[-1] + 1, 2126))
    for year in years:
        ratio = (1 + r / 100) / (1 + g / 100) * ratio + nx / 100       # equation (5) divided by GDP
        path.append(100 * ratio)
        if ratio < -1 and passed.endswith("2125"):
            passed = f"above 100% of GDP from {year}"
    low = -200 if min(path + [f_star]) > -190 else -700                 # a wider axis only for very large debts
    fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=history.index, y=history, mode="lines", name="BEA data", line=dict(color=GRAY, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=path, mode="lines", name="Projection", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1900, 2200], y=[f_star, f_star], mode="lines", name="Long run, f*",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_hline(y=-100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Long run: f* = {f_star:.1f}% of GDP; net foreign debt {passed}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", range=[1970, 2130]), yaxis=dict(title="Percent of GDP", range=[low, 20]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))
    return fig


interact(debt_projection,
         nx=FloatSlider(value=-3.0, min=-6.0, max=0.0, step=0.5, description="trade balance nx, % of GDP", style=WIDE),
         g=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=3.0, max=7.0, step=0.5, description="nominal GDP growth g, %", style=WIDE),
         r=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="return on the debt r, %", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** A calculator built on the foreign-debt dynamics of the Model overview, equations (5) and (7), and the BEA data of Fig. 6, adapted from the discussion of foreign debt in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The title reads $f^* = -78.0$ percent: the debt ratio keeps rising, but slowly, from 70.9 percent toward 78.0
percent of GDP (it is still at 75.3 percent in 2050). Solving equation (7) for the trade balance that holds today's
ratio,

$$nx = f\,\frac{\bar{g} - \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}} = -0.709 \times \frac{0.04}{1.04} = -0.0273,$$

a deficit of about 2.7 percent of GDP keeps the net foreign debt at its 2025 level. The current deficit is only a
little larger.

**(b)** With $\bar{r} = 2$, the slider shows $f^* = -104.0$ percent at $nx = -2.0$ and $-78.0$ percent at
$nx = -1.5$. Exactly, with $f^* = -1$:

$$nx = -1 \times \frac{0.04 - 0.02}{1.04} = -0.0192.$$

The deficit must not exceed 1.92 percent of GDP, about two thirds of today's deficit. A positive return on the debt
adds interest to the borrowing, so the same debt ceiling allows a smaller trade deficit.

**(c)** Equation (7) gives $f^* = 1.03 \times (-0.03)/(0.03 - 0.02) = -3.09$: the debt heads toward 309 percent of GDP,
and the calculator shows it passing 100 percent of GDP in 2039. The long-run ratio of equation (7) has
$\bar{g} - \bar{r}$ in its denominator: with the same deficit of 3 percent, $f^*$ is $-156$ percent when $\bar{g} = 4$ and
$\bar{r} = 2$, so halving the gap from 2 points to 1 point roughly doubles the debt. The factor
$\frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}} = 1.02/1.03 = 0.990$ is also close to one, so the ratio drifts for a very long time
before it settles. If $\bar{r}$ reached $\bar{g}$, no stable ratio would exist, and equation (6)
says that such a path cannot last. The code below confirms the numbers:

```python
f_2025 = share_of_gdp(us.niip, us.gdp).dropna().iloc[-1] / 100
print(f"(a) f* = {100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(-0.03, 0.04):.1f}%; the balance that holds {100 * f_2025:.1f}% "
      f"is {100 * f_2025 * 0.04 / 1.04:.2f}% of GDP")
nx_max = -1.0 * (0.04 - 0.02) / (1 + 0.04)               # equation (7) solved for nx, with f* = -1
print(f"(b) largest deficit {-100 * nx_max:.2f}% of GDP; check: f* = "
      f"{100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(nx_max, 0.04, 0.02):.1f}%")
ratio, crossing = f_2025, 0
for year in range(2026, 2126):
    ratio = 1.02 / 1.03 * ratio - 0.03                     # equation (5) divided by GDP
    if ratio < -1 and crossing == 0:
        crossing = year
print(f"(c) f* = {100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(-0.03, 0.03, 0.02):.1f}%; the debt passes 100% of GDP in {crossing}")
```

It prints `(a) f* = -78.0%; the balance that holds -70.9% is -2.73% of GDP`, then a largest deficit of 1.92 percent
(with $f^* = -100.0$), and $f^* = -309.0$ percent with a crossing in 2039.

</details>

**Problem 9 (Challenge): When the South grows.** In the North–South model of the Model overview, let the South's
workforce $L_s$ grow while all the other numbers stay the same. Think of a large economy with many workers joining
world trade, as China did when it entered the World Trade Organization in 2001
([WTO](https://www.wto.org/english/news_e/pres01_e/pr252_e.htm)). The calculator compares consumption per person
under free trade with autarky (autarky = 100) for each good and each country; the numbers on the green bars are the
amounts per person. Answer with its slider.

(a) Move $L_s$ from 400 to 600. What happens to the world price of a computer, to apples per person in the North and
to computers per person in the South?

(b) Use equations (10) and (11) to find the range of $L_s$ for which complete specialization is the outcome, given
the other numbers. What happens to the South's gain from trade at the upper end of the range?

(c) A northern politician says that the South's growth hurts the North; a southern politician says that a bigger
South is better for southern workers. Who is right in this model? Show that the South's total consumption of
computers does not depend on $L_s$, and explain why in words.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Equation (10) gives the world price as a function of $L_s$. Put it into each inequality of condition (11) and solve
each one for $L_s$. For (c), multiply the South's computers per person, $x_s/(2p)$, by the number of southern workers,
and think about what an apple buys on the world market.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def south_grows(L_s=400):
    """Equations (8) to (11): consumption per person with free trade, relative to autarky, for any size of the South."""
    closed = pd.DataFrame({"North": autarky(x_n, z_n, L_n), "South": autarky(x_s, z_s, L_s)})
    trade = free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s)
    p = trade.loc["Price of a computer, p (apples)", "North"]
    labels, index, text = [], [], []
    for country in ["North", "South"]:
        for good in ["Apples", "Computers"]:
            amount = trade.loc[good + " per person", country]
            labels.append(f"{country}: {good.lower()}")
            index.append(100 * amount / closed.loc[good + " per person", country])
            text.append(f"{amount:.0f}" if good == "Apples" else f"{amount:.2f}")     # the amount per person
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=labels, y=[100, 100, 100, 100], name="Autarky", marker_color=GRAY))
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=labels, y=index, name="Free trade", marker_color=GREEN, text=text, textposition="outside"))
    note = f"between the autarky prices {x_n / z_n:.0f} and {x_s / z_s:.0f}"             # condition (11)
    if p >= x_s / z_s:
        note = "the South's gain from trade is gone"
    fig.update_layout(title=f"L_s = {L_s}: a computer costs {p:.1f} apples, {note}", barmode="group",
                      yaxis=dict(title="Consumption per person, autarky = 100", range=[0, 600]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.98, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(south_grows, L_s=IntSlider(value=400, min=200, max=800, step=50, description="southern workers L_s", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** A calculator built on the `autarky` and `free_trade` functions of "Model in code", adapted from the apple-and-computer example in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** From $L_s = 400$ to $600$ the world price of a computer rises from 25.0 to 37.5 apples. Northern workers eat
300 apples instead of 200 (the bar goes from 250 to 375), and still have 8 computers. Southern workers still eat 50
apples, but have 1.33 computers instead of 2.00.

**(b)** By equation (10), $p = L_s x_s/(L_n z_n) = 100\,L_s/1{,}600 = L_s/16$. Condition (11) has two parts:

$$\frac{x_s}{z_s} > p \;\Longleftrightarrow\; 50 > \frac{L_s}{16} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; L_s < \frac{L_n z_n}{z_s} = 800,
\qquad
p > \frac{x_n}{z_n} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \frac{L_s}{16} > 10 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; L_s > \frac{L_n x_n}{x_s} = 160.$$

So the North makes only computers and the South only apples for $160 < L_s < 800$. As $L_s$ approaches 800, the world
price rises to 50 apples, the South's own autarky price, and southern computers per person fall to
$x_s/(2p) = 100/100 = 1$, the autarky level: the South's gain from trade disappears. With an even larger South,
southern workers would also make computers, the price would stay at 50, and all the gains from trade would go to the
North.

**(c)** In this model the northern politician is wrong: each northerner's apples, $L_s x_s/(2L_n)$, rise with $L_s$,
and computers stay at $z_n/2 = 8$. The southern politician is wrong too: a bigger South is worse for each southern
worker. Apples stay at $x_s/2 = 50$, but computers per person, $L_n z_n/(2L_s)$, fall as $L_s$ grows, so each
worker's gain from trade shrinks, although nobody falls below the autarky bundle.
The South's total computers are

$$L_s \times \frac{x_s}{2p} = L_s \times \frac{L_n z_n}{2L_s} = \frac{L_n z_n}{2} = 800,$$

half of the world's computers, whatever the size of the South. The extra southern workers make more apples, but each
apple buys fewer computers on the world market, in the same proportion: the price of what the South sells falls
relative to the price of what it buys. The South gets more apples, but no more computers. (In reality, as the
free-migration block of the Model overview notes, switching jobs is costly, so northern workers in the industries that
compete with imports can lose even when the North as a whole gains.) The code below confirms the numbers:

```python
for workers in [400, 600, 800]:
    world_trade = free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, workers)
    p = world_trade.loc["Price of a computer, p (apples)", "North"]
    north_apples = world_trade.loc["Apples per person", "North"]
    south_computers = world_trade.loc["Computers per person", "South"]
    print(f"L_s = {workers}: p = {p:.1f}, North apples {north_apples:.0f}, South computers {south_computers:.2f} "
          f"each and {workers * south_computers:.0f} in total")
print(f"Complete specialization for {L_n * x_n / x_s:.0f} < L_s < {L_n * z_n / z_s:.0f}")
```

It prints `L_s = 400: p = 25.0, North apples 200, South computers 2.00 each and 800 in total`, then 37.5, 300, 1.33
and 800 for 600 workers, 50.0, 400, 1.00 and 800 for 800 workers, and the range 160 < L_s < 800.

</details>
